forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state an effect: a single compiler rating without a measured water outcome or a stated mechanism [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1626_2014_harvesting_collection_of_water]. Any effect would be off-site for farmers, arriving downstream or at landscape scale rather than on their plots. What is missing is a second independent source or one measured finding.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: The Niger compiler rates assisted natural regeneration as lowering wind velocity, a shelter effect of regenerated woody cover [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1626_2014_wind_velocity].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: This is a single practitioner rating of everyday wind speed, not of cyclone or storm damage.

forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: Restoring forest rebuilds the habitat that native species depend on, and the gain is moderate overall. A meta-analysis across 221 study landscapes found forest restoration enhances biodiversity by 15–84% and vegetation structure by 36–77% compared with degraded ecosystems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1], and a meta-analysis of terrestrial restoration found restored sites had 20% higher mean biodiversity than unrestored sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1]. Natural regeneration outperforms active planting: restoration success for biodiversity was 34 to 56% higher [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1]. In Brazil restored areas, regardless of technique, show higher diversity than agricultural land and pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_2], and tree species richness rises with time since disturbance [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1]. Woody species richness in Senegal exclosures rose from 27 species at 1 year to 51 at 5 and 12 years [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1], and Ethiopian authors credit afforestation and area closures with improving biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. Compilers in Afghanistan, Bangladesh and India report animal, plant and habitat diversity rising under protection and regeneration [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity], and protection and community management retain forest cover [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. A global study of natural climate solutions, citing an earlier assessment, lists biodiversity habitat among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].
forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: The sub-practices do not all agree. One review names a harm: where forests can regenerate naturally, reforestation by tree planting can reduce biodiversity benefits if the species or management chosen do not provide suitable habitat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_williams24_1]. Some units found no gain: abundance in restored systems often does not differ from pasture and agricultural land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_3], there was no clear-cut evidence that a Vietnamese forest project helped biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1], and management transfers in Madagascar remained superficial while clearing continued [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]. The terrestrial restoration meta-analysis pools forest with non-forest ecosystems and natural with assisted restoration [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1]. Many supporting units are compiler ratings or forest-cover change standing in for biodiversity, and the Ethiopian result is a qualitative report from a bundled watershed programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. The global co-benefit listing is second-hand and gives no size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].

forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, closing land to cutting and grazing and protecting forest strongly raises biodiversity. In Senegal, woody species richness in village exclosures rose from 27 species in a 1-year exclosure to 51 species in 5- and 12-year exclosures, more than 52% higher [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. In an Ethiopian watershed, the authors report improved biodiversity through afforestation and area closures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. Compilers report that migratory animals and birds returned to protected land in Afghanistan [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity], that habitat and animal diversity increased with canopy cover and tree density in Bangladesh [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_animal_diversity], and that Indian community forests provide more water and habitat for small animals and birds, with plant diversity up through better moisture, soil and microclimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity]. In Bolivia four of the payment-like initiatives showed marked environmental protection effects [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1]. Community management retained forest cover in Nepal, India and Bolivia [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3], and environmental condition improved in 56% of community-forest cases worldwide [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1].
forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Two units found no gain: management transfers in Madagascar remained superficial and did not stop clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]. In the global community-forest review condition decreased in 32% of cases [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], and in Bolivia two initiatives had intermediate and three weak protection effects [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1]. The only measured species count is the Senegal study, which compares exclosures of different ages rather than closed with open land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. The rest are compiler ratings, a qualitative report from a bundled watershed programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2], a rapid qualitative rating of payment schemes, and forest-cover change standing in for biodiversity.

forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: This row rests on forest-governance evidence pooled across several countries, with forest cover standing in for habitat. A meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation (SMD = −0.12) compared with areas without payments [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2]. World Bank participatory forest management projects reported reduced deforestation rates, regeneration of degraded forests and protection of biodiversity where those outcomes were monitored, and Bank-supported payment schemes had a positive effect on deforestation in some countries [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg13_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1].
forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: The payment schemes were applied broadly rather than targeting high-value forest areas, which limits what they deliver for biodiversity [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1]. Most units measure forest cover or deforestation, a component proxy for biodiversity, not species. The pooled payment effects come from a systematic review and meta-analysis, while the World Bank units are evaluation narratives that cover only projects that monitored outcomes; all concern keeping or managing existing forest through payments or community management rather than restoration planting.

forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In these upper-middle-income settings the evidence is about succession on land that has been cleared or degraded, and about what speeds it up. A meta-analysis of Brazilian restored biomes finds that restored areas, regardless of the restoration technique, show higher diversity metrics than degraded areas such as agricultural lands and pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_2]. Tree species richness rose as a function of time since disturbance across an Atlantic rainforest chronosequence [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1], with a forest estimated to need 65 years, range 23 to 178, to reach a proportion of 80% animal-dispersed species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_2]. Assisted recruitment shortens the wait: beneath framework-species plantings in Thai dry forest, tree seedlings of many species recruited, 25 of them animal-dispersed and 11 wind-dispersed [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1], and artificial perches produced native zoochoric regenerants that were absent from planted rings, so bringing in dispersers mattered more than the planting itself [ev_biodiversity_outcome_loureiro21_1]. On Turkmen barkhan sands the compiler records that the vegetation now provides the habitat for 25-27 species of plants and animals and rates habitat diversity as increased [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_habitat_diversity]. Holding the cover is the companion mechanism: under community forest management in the Sierra Norte de Puebla, forest cover did not decline after the handover but increased by 8% [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1].
forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: The direction is consistent. Beyond the Brazilian meta-analysis the base is chronosequences and site studies, a compiler rating, and a forest-cover change read from land-use maps as a proxy for habitat rather than a count of species [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. In the same Brazilian meta-analysis, abundance in restored systems often did not differ from that in pastures and agricultural lands; the authors treat abundance as a poor indicator of recovery, so this null does not cut against the diversity gain [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_3]. Where a project was independently evaluated the result was less flattering — biodiversity is hard to assess, the management-effectiveness tool used was not a suitable proxy, and there was no clear-cut evidence that a Vietnamese special-use forest project improved biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1]. Time is the binding condition: the Atlantic-forest estimate spans decades to well over a century before the assemblage approaches the composition of a mature forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_2], so nothing here promises a measurable result inside a project cycle. Read the gains with care. The gains are measured against the degraded or cleared starting point, not against intact forest, and a young stand holding less than old-growth is incomplete recovery rather than loss. And the perch and framework-species findings are about assisting dispersal into a restoration site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_loureiro21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1]: they presuppose a seed source within reach, which is a siting condition a scan can test and a restoration in a cleared landscape may fail.

forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: Restoring forest cover rebuilds the carbon stored in trees and soil that cleared or degraded land lacks. A global meta-analysis puts natural regeneration removal rates at 9.1–18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. A pantropical synthesis of field plots gives above-ground biomass growth in naturally regrowing secondary forest, for example 7.6 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year in younger African rainforest stands and 0.5 in older subtropical Asian mountain stands [ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_22]. A global model puts the average rate of natural forest regrowth at 3.16 Mg C per hectare per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_2]. Planting native trees on former pasture in Brazil built up 21.85, 25.78 and 38.29 Mg/ha of carbon in successively older plantings [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3]. Protection and community forest management keep carbon in standing forest by retaining cover, measured as forest-cover change in payment schemes, community forests and GEF sites [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1]. A global model of natural climate solutions finds reforestation is the largest natural pathway, with a maximum mitigation potential, under food, fibre and biodiversity safeguards, of 2.7–17.9 Pg CO2e per year (95% confidence interval) [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1].
forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The gain is moderate rather than large, and much of the size evidence is not a fresh measurement. The IPCC values are compiled default tables carried forward from earlier guidance with a stated uncertainty of plus or minus 90% and no sample size [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_4], the global regrowth rates are model outputs for above-ground carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_2], the plot synthesis and IPCC tables report dry matter, not carbon, and the global reforestation figure is a model of total potential across the world, not a per-hectare rate, with a wide range that its authors call highly uncertain [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1]. One source names a harm: afforestation on peaty soils can lead to losses of soil carbon that outweigh that sequestered as the trees grow [ev_carbon_sequestration_seddon21_7], so organic and peat soils need separate treatment. Four units found no gain: soil carbon under forest did not increase significantly over cropland in the first 0–5 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_5], a REDD+ pilot in Nepal had no significant effect on forest carbon in community forests [ev_carbon_sequestration_snilstveit19_1], and in Madagascar transfer of management to communities remained superficial while clearing continued [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]. Forest cover and soil carbon enter as parts of the carbon picture, not direct measures of it, and practitioner ratings make up several of the agreeing units.

forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: The same carbon mechanism applies in these low- and lower-middle-income contexts: community and participatory forest management programmes that restore degraded forest have been associated with improved environmental condition and biomass gains — one expert-rated case on degraded forestland reported increased above-ground biomass, especially on pastoral and silvopastoral land.
forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: One Nepal REDD+ pilot found an insignificant effect on total forest carbon, and Madagascar case studies found community forest-transfer arrangements remained superficial and failed to halt resource degradation by clearing — so the gain depends on how genuinely the management transfer and protection are implemented, not on restoration being designated alone.

forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: This row pools evidence whose settings span several income groups. Naturally regrowing secondary forest adds above-ground biomass year after year: a pantropical synthesis of field plots gives mean growth of 2.4 to 7.6 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year in younger stands across tropical and subtropical zones, and 0.5 to 3.5 in older stands [ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_22, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_2]. IPCC default tables add drier zones, from 0.2–0.7 tonnes in young African tropical shrublands to 5.0 in continental Asia [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_3]. Forest governance keeps carbon in standing forest: a meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation against comparison areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2], and World Bank participatory forest management projects reported reduced deforestation and regeneration of degraded forests where those outcomes were monitored [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1].
forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The growth figures are biomass in dry matter, not carbon, and none is a with-and-without comparison; they describe how fast regrowth adds biomass, not the gain over an unrestored site. In a few zone and age combinations of the plot synthesis the interval includes zero [ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_14, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_8]. The IPCC dryland figures are compiled defaults carried forward from earlier guidance with a stated uncertainty of plus or minus 90% and no sample size [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_1]. The governance units measure forest cover, not carbon, and concern keeping existing forest through payments or community management rather than restoration; the payment schemes were applied broadly rather than targeting high-value forest areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1], and the World Bank units are evaluation narratives covering only projects that monitored outcomes.

forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings the measured evidence is a native-species restoration on former pasture in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, which stored 21.85, 25.78 and 38.29 Mg of carbon per hectare at three, five and seven years [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3]. Under community forest management in Mexico's Sierra Norte de Puebla forest cover did not undergo any loss and increased by 8%, which enters here as retained and added cover rather than a carbon stock [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1].
forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The class is slight: the evidence is a single Brazilian planting chronosequence and a Mexican cover reading. The same Atlantic-forest study measured 138.94 Mg of carbon per hectare in the mature forest, so the seven-year planting is far from its reference: that is incomplete recovery against intact forest, while the removal claimed is against the pasture the planting replaced [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3]. The Mexican result is a before-and-after reading of land-use maps with no counterfactual, a proxy for carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. Soil carbon is not covered in this income band.

forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: At long-term ecological research sites in the USA, forest succession and declining evapotranspiration may explain increased summer streamflow at two temperate forest sites that were logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. Against it, a cited New Zealand study notes that afforestation can provide relevant erosion reduction benefits while reducing water yield [ev_water_regulation_iufro18_4].
forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: What separates the two is the practice and the time scale: the gain is summer flow at sites logged in the early nineteenth century and left to forest succession, while the loss is afforestation, cited without a time frame [ev_water_yield_jon12_3, ev_water_regulation_iufro18_4]. Both are thin. The US attribution is tentative in the authors' own wording, and no intervention is described at those sites; the New Zealand unit is a modelled trade-off carried from a study the assessment cites. Neither gives a size, and neither comes from the low- and lower-middle-income target. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment.

forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: In the lower-income contexts in this scope, the gain-side evidence reads the other way from the pooled syntheses: baseflow from Ethiopian catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than baseflow from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], and a regional land-climate model projects a significant 84.9% increase in water yield for the Irrawaddy under full reforestation potential by mid-century [ev_water_regulation_teo22_4]. One unit runs against them: an essay on Himalayan deforestation states that as forest regrows after cutting, its evapotranspiration rises and stream water yield decreases to approach pre-cutting levels in 6-12 years [ev_water_yield_ham87_3].
forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more. Neither gain measures restored forest against the land it replaced: the Ethiopian figure compares exclosure catchments with cropland, and the Irrawaddy figure is a mid-century model scenario at landscape scale, not a project observation. The opposing unit describes regrowth of a logged forest, following an example from a logged stream in Queensland, so it is recovery from a recent cut, not restoration of degraded land, and its setting is not clearly lower-income [ev_water_yield_ham87_3]. Read it alongside the unscoped catchment water yield row, which pools the wider measured evidence, before treating restoration in a lower-income catchment as a source of extra downstream water.

forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: There is not enough evidence to rate this. Two reviews point to less water leaving the catchment after forest is planted or restored. The first states that scientific evidence typically highlights substantial losses in streamflow following afforestation and reforestation, while clearing forest increases streamflow [ev_water_yield_ellison17_1]. The other explains that tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, which evaporates before reaching the soil, and that trees use much of the water that does soak in [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1].
forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: Both are review statements that report other studies, with no measured size [ev_water_yield_ellison17_1, ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. The first review also cites a counter-example [ev_water_yield_ellison17_1], and the second says extensive reforestation should not be expected to raise dry-season flows [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. A measured catchment result from a restoration project is needed before a rating can be given. This row concerns how much water leaves the catchment for downstream users, not whether the restored land itself holds more.

forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: In China the evidence is modelled. A regional land-climate model under full reforestation potential projects statistically significant water-yield increases of 11.4% on the Loess Plateau–North China Plain, 16.9% on the Yangtze Plain and 17.6% in Southeast China [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_2, ev_water_regulation_teo22_3], and in the headwater of the Heihe River Basin a 12.6% increase in forest cover due to spruce reforestation was predicted to increase annual runoff by 8.6% [ev_water_yield_zhang17_6].
forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: Every unit is a projection: the gains are scenario results for full reforestation potential, the Heihe figure is cited from an earlier modelling study, and the regional model works through precipitation as well as evapotranspiration, not only through what the trees use [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6]. Read the class as what large reforestation could do in modelled scenarios, not as a measured project outcome. The one programme result from China, the review report that Grain-for-Green planting with mainly fast-growing non-native species reduced water supply, has been re-homed to the plantation family, which is parked out of the forest-restoration roll-up; it remains the warning on species choice, and that row should be read before assuming a gain. All units are from China. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment.

forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: Cost per hectare depends mainly on method: modelled implementation cost has a median of US$140/ha for natural regeneration [ev_project_cost_busch24_1], and natural regeneration methods are cited at US$12-3,880/ha against US$105-25,830/ha for restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics [ev_project_cost_williams24_2]. A Brazilian cost survey reports the same gap: direct seeding and seedling planting cost approximately ten times more (about US$2000/ha) than natural and assisted regeneration and enrichment planting (about US$200/ha), mostly due to the higher input costs [ev_project_cost_branc19_1, ev_project_cost_branc19_2, ev_project_cost_branc19_3]. A World Bank irrigation and watershed project in Madagascar estimated US$1,500 per hectare for reforested area, against $300 per hectare for avoided deforestation [ev_project_cost_exact14_1]. The opportunity cost of land (median US$4,807/ha) is generally higher and more variable than implementation cost [ev_project_cost_busch24_5].
forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: Most reported figures state no price year, some are assumptions rather than observed costs [ev_project_cost_wri17_1], the Madagascar figure is a planning estimate used in a carbon-accounting tool's worked example, not a measured cost [ev_project_cost_exact14_1], and WOCAT values are compiler-entered conversions from local currency. Values from high-income and upper-middle-income settings, including the Brazilian survey figures, are excluded from the low- and lower-middle-income range. Plantation costs sit in their own family rows and do not count toward forest restoration.

forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings the reported costs are large overall, but lowest where existing regrowth is used: assisted natural regeneration in Niger at US$90/ha and in Bangladesh at US$197.62/ha [ev_project_cost_wocat_2325_2017_establishment, ev_project_cost_wocat_4372_2019_establishment]. Planting-based work costs more: broadleaf plantations in India at US$758.08/ha [ev_project_cost_wocat_5243_2019_establishment], rain forest corridor planting in Madagascar at US$938/ha [ev_project_cost_wri17_4], community forest management in Benin at US$1362/ha [ev_project_cost_wri17_2], reforestation in a planned Madagascar watershed component at US$1,500 per hectare [ev_project_cost_exact14_1], the Khost learning site in Afghanistan at US$1810.44/ha [ev_project_cost_wocat_7460_2024_establishment], and community microbasin reforestation in Honduras at US$5,402.39/ha [ev_project_cost_wocat_750_2016_establishment].
forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: None of the figures states a price year. The practitioner values are converted from local-currency entries [ev_project_cost_wocat_2325_2017_establishment, ev_project_cost_wocat_750_2016_establishment]. The Madagascar watershed figure is a planning estimate for a World Bank project, not recorded spending [ev_project_cost_exact14_1].

forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: Within upper-middle-income evidence, Brazil's national cost survey finds the same gap as elsewhere: direct seeding and seedling planting cost approximately ten times more (about US$2000 per hectare) than the less intensive approaches, natural and assisted regeneration and enrichment planting grouped together (about US$200 per hectare), mostly because of the higher input costs [ev_project_cost_branc19_1, ev_project_cost_branc19_2, ev_project_cost_branc19_3]. A WOCAT-compiled Bosnian karst afforestation technology reports a much higher establishment cost of US$6,078.79 per hectare [ev_project_cost_wocat_4367_2019_establishment]. A World Resources Institute table of Latin American and Caribbean restoration costs lists assisted natural regeneration in Brazil at US$639 per hectare, reforestation with eucalyptus and native species in Brazil at US$2,900 per hectare, and reforestation with native species in Colombia at US$1,060 per hectare [ev_project_cost_wri17_6, ev_project_cost_wri17_7, ev_project_cost_wri17_9].
forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: The ~US$200 figure is stated for natural regeneration, assisted regeneration and enrichment planting together, not for natural regeneration alone, and both Brazilian figures exclude the opportunity cost of land and long-run maintenance, which the survey's own authors say makes their numbers certainly underestimate the true cost [ev_project_cost_branc19_1, ev_project_cost_branc19_2, ev_project_cost_branc19_3]. The WOCAT figure is a compiler-entered conversion from local currency with no cross-sheet price-year normalisation [ev_project_cost_wocat_4367_2019_establishment]. The World Resources Institute figures are secondary citations of other named studies collected into a summary table, with no price year stated [ev_project_cost_wri17_6, ev_project_cost_wri17_7, ev_project_cost_wri17_9]. All of this is upper-middle income (Brazil, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Colombia); none of it has been checked against a low- or lower-middle-income setting.

forest_restoration__cost_per_tco2e_avoid.mechanism: Abatement cost compares implementation and land opportunity costs with the carbon gained: modelled natural regeneration costs a median of US$23.80 per tCO2 [ev_project_cost_busch24_3]. In Colombia's western Andes a median carbon price of US$1.99 per tCO2 over 30 years was enough to compensate landowners for letting pastures regenerate [ev_project_cost_chazdon16_1], and conserving 90% of remaining mangroves could be achieved at carbon prices between 3.0 and 13.0 US$ per tCO2 [ev_project_cost_jakovac20_2]. Two payment schemes report low programme costs per tonne of carbon: the PAS scheme in Brazil was estimated at 0.56 USD per ton of CO2, and the Ugandan scheme cost $0.57 per ton of delayed emissions against an estimated social benefit of $1.11 per ton, roughly two times the cost [ev_project_cost_snilstveit19_2, ev_project_cost_snilstveit19_3].
forest_restoration__cost_per_tco2e_avoid.conditionality: All units are modelled or break-even prices rather than project budgets, and the mangrove conservation figure concerns avoided emissions from protecting existing forest rather than restoration; the Colombian figure is cited from another study and states no price year. The Brazilian figure is a total programme cost given without assessing cost-effectiveness, both payment figures are cited in a systematic review, and both concern paying landholders to keep existing forest rather than restoring it [ev_project_cost_snilstveit19_2, ev_project_cost_snilstveit19_3]. Plantation results are reported in their own family rows and no longer count toward forest restoration.

forest_restoration__cost_reduction.mechanism: Most of the evidence says letting forest regrow is cheaper to establish than planting it. A global study of natural regeneration, citing earlier work, puts natural regeneration at US$12–3,880 per ha against US$105–25,830 for forest restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics [ev_project_cost_williams24_1], and reforestation guidelines list lower cost among the benefits of natural regeneration [ev_project_cost_stanturf26_1]. In a Mexican dry-forest planting trial, polyethylene mulch cut the cost per established plant, including the nursery, from US$18.00 on bare soil to US$2.45, because far more plants survived (92 of 180 against 10 of 180) [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1]. Pointing the other way, a global study of natural climate solutions, citing earlier work, says reforestation can incur high costs of establishment [ev_project_cost_griscom17_5].
forest_restoration__cost_reduction.conditionality: No source gives a usable cost figure for this practice as a whole, so no cost class is given. The per-hectare ranges are a second-hand comparison spanning very different projects [ev_project_cost_williams24_1], the guideline statement is an expert view without a number [ev_project_cost_stanturf26_1], the Mexican figures are per plant at a single site and cannot be scaled to a per-hectare or programme cost [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1], and the high-cost statement has no figure [ev_project_cost_griscom17_5]. Only the Mexican trial is a measurement, and it comes from an upper-middle-income country.

forest_restoration__cost_reduction__inco.mechanism: Measures taken at planting can cut the cost of each tree that survives. In a Mexican tropical dry forest, polyethylene mulch raised establishment from 10 of 180 unmulched plants to 92 of 180 and brought the cost per established plant down from USD 18.00 to USD 2.45, nursery costs included; alfalfa straw and leaf litter cost more material and established fewer plants, at USD 12.50 and USD 13.33 per plant [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1]. At the other end of the scale, a successful black-mangrove project in Tabasco reforested 50 ha at USD 3,945.60 per hectare, a figure that covers sanitation, dredging, soil conservation works, ridge restoration, training, plant production, transplanting and monitoring [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_2].
forest_restoration__cost_reduction__inco.conditionality: The two figures are not comparable and neither is a cost saving on its own: the mulch result is a cost per surviving plant from a single trial on three species, while the mangrove figure is a whole-project cost per hectare for one site, reported in a diagnostic study without a comparison against a cheaper alternative [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1, ev_project_cost_hernmel17_2]. Both come from Mexico, an upper-middle-income setting, so they say little about what the same works would cost elsewhere, and the mangrove cost is a second-hand figure attributed to a local project record [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_2].

forest_restoration__cross_family__biodiv.mechanism: Across restoration approaches, restored land holds moderately more biodiversity than degraded land. A meta-analysis across 221 study landscapes found forest restoration enhances biodiversity by 15–84% and vegetation structure by 36–77% compared with degraded ecosystems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1], and a meta-analysis of terrestrial restoration found restored sites had 20% higher mean biodiversity than unrestored sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1]. In Brazil, restored areas, regardless of technique, show higher diversity than agricultural land and pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_2], and in an Ethiopian watershed the authors report improved biodiversity through afforestation and area closures where the measures matched the landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. A global study of natural climate solutions, citing an earlier assessment, lists biodiversity habitat among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].
forest_restoration__cross_family__biodiv.conditionality: Richness gains do not always mean more wildlife: in the Brazilian dataset abundance in restored systems often did not differ from pasture and agricultural land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_3]. Restored sites also stay short of intact ecosystems: biodiversity was on average 13% lower than at reference sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_2]; that comparison is with the target ecosystem, not the degraded starting point, so it is held out of the class as a recovery shortfall. The terrestrial meta-analysis pools forest with non-forest ecosystems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1], and the Ethiopian result is a qualitative report from a bundled watershed programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. The global co-benefit listing is second-hand and gives no size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].

forest_restoration__cross_family__carbon.mechanism: Returning degraded or cropped land to forest stores carbon in biomass and soil as woody vegetation and litter build up. A meta-analysis of Brazilian restored biomes finds that restored areas, regardless of the restoration technique, hold more carbon than degraded agricultural lands and pastures [ev_carbon_sequestration_jakovac24_1]. A meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones found that returning cropland or bare land to forest raised soil organic carbon content by 25.28% compared with cropland [ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_3]. A global model of natural climate solutions finds reforestation, which there includes both planting and assisted regeneration, is the largest natural pathway, with a maximum mitigation potential under safeguards of 2.7–17.9 Pg CO2e per year (95% confidence interval) [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__carbon.conditionality: Soil storage takes time to show: in the erosion-zone meta-analysis there was no significant increase in soil organic carbon under forestland compared with cropland in the first 0–5 years, so the removal is not something a short project will see in its soils [ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_5]. Neither meta-analysis, nor the global model, separates planting from natural regeneration, so the gain cannot be credited to a particular restoration family [ev_carbon_sequestration_jakovac24_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_3]. The Brazilian result is a carbon stock compared with degraded references rather than a net balance of removals, the soil figure is a change in carbon content rather than a stock, and neither comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. The removals are a climate benefit, off-site for the farmer. The global figure is a modelled worldwide total, not a per-hectare rate, and its authors call it highly uncertain [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1].

forest_restoration__cross_family__catchm.mechanism: A global systematic review pooling forest restoration with forestry and afforestation found that annual water yield decreased in about 80% of study cases reporting it and increased in 6% [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1], baseflow decreased in 63% of cases [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2], groundwater levels or recharge decreased in 67% of the studies reporting them [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1], and no water-yield gains were observed in the meta-analysed subset [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3]. A global review of forest change found a significant negative relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3], and another review states that evidence typically highlights substantial losses in streamflow following afforestation and reforestation [ev_water_yield_ellison17_1]. Tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, which evaporates without reaching soil water reserves, and much of the water that does soak in is used by the trees themselves [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__catchm.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more, and a loss here can coexist with a local gain in the water stress rows [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. The syntheses read scale differently: in the systematic review the decrease shrinks at larger time and space scales [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3], while the global review found no significant relationship in small watersheds and a significant reduction only in large ones [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2, ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The same global review records a minority of watersheds where runoff increased with forest cover gain [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5]. The reviews pool restoration with other forest cover gain; the systematic review reports vote counts rather than sizes, is dominated by temperate and Oceania studies, and the baseflow cases are few [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2]. One further unit is carried but does not vote: by 25 to 35 years after forest harvest in temperate basins, summer streamflow declined by up to 30%–50% relative to the reference basins [ev_water_yield_jon12_1]; its comparison is with intact old forest, so it is a recovery shortfall and is kept out of the class.

forest_restoration__cross_family__cost_p.mechanism: Across restoration families, the opportunity cost of land is generally higher and more variable than implementation cost, with a modelled median of US$4,807/ha [ev_project_cost_busch24_5]; restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics are cited at US$105-25,830/ha [ev_project_cost_williams24_2] and the TEEB study assumed US$2,390-3,450/ha [ev_project_cost_wri17_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__cost_p.conditionality: These are modelled, cited or assumed values rather than observed project costs, none states a price year, and they pool restoration methods without separating families.

forest_restoration__cross_family__cost_r.mechanism: There is not enough evidence here to say whether restoration costs are low or high. The only source, a global study of natural climate solutions citing earlier work, says reforestation may involve trade-offs with other land uses and can incur high costs of establishment [ev_project_cost_griscom17_5].
forest_restoration__cross_family__cost_r.conditionality: The statement is second-hand and gives no figure, place or unit [ev_project_cost_griscom17_5]. A second independent source, or a measured cost, would be needed to state a class.

forest_restoration__cross_family__drough.mechanism: A meta-analysis of catchment restoration in Ethiopia reports that exclosures, tree planting, bunds and terraces reduce water losses and improve the quantity and quality of water in soils, rivers and aquifers, a pathway to drought resilience [ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__drough.conditionality: This is a single source on soil and stream water, a component of drought impact rather than a drought outcome, and it pools exclosure and planting with soil and water conservation structures, so the share due to tree restoration is not isolated [ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1].

forest_restoration__cross_family__flood_.mechanism: Restored forest cover lowers flood peaks in this evidence by a moderate amount. A systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds peak flow changes by roughly half the change in forest cover, so a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium and large catchments, which the review attributes to forests detaining floodwater through infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1]. A global systematic review of forest restoration and water found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies with data on them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. A harvest experiment in Oregon adds a measured recovery: after clear-cutting, peak discharges recovered gradually over time as the basin revegetated, which the authors attribute to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. A global study of natural climate solutions also lists flood control among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits, citing an earlier assessment, with no size given [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3].
forest_restoration__cross_family__flood_.conditionality: The flood-cover review pools afforestation, reforestation, woodland and deforestation cases and its peak-flow points come from modelled scenarios in mostly temperate catchments, so its rule of thumb is a synthesis of other studies' models [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1]. The restoration-and-water review pools explicit and implicit forest restoration with forestry and afforestation and reports vote counts rather than effect sizes, so it does not say how large the reduction is or which restoration practice delivers it [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. The Oregon recovery is measured against the freshly cut state in a harvest study, not against long-degraded land, and the paper does not say whether the regrowth was planted or natural [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. No unit comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. Expert positions point the other way: an FAO–CIFOR synthesis concludes that massive forestation programmes proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may bring other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. A review of coastal tree belts adds a coastal null: the science on short-period wave damping should not be taken to show that vegetation can reduce the effects of storm surges [ev_flood_hazard_feagin10_1]; it concerns coastal plantings rather than river floods. The co-benefit listing is second-hand and states no size, place or scale [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3]. None of these is a measurement; what separates them from the evidence of lower peaks is that they address flood prevention at large scale, while the reviews and the Oregon basin report peak flows in study catchments. No unit covers severe or extreme flood. For farmers the effect is off-site.

forest_restoration__cross_family__flood_.mechanism: Restored forest cover lowers flood peaks by a moderate amount in this evidence. A systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds peak flow changes by roughly half the change in forest cover, so a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium and large catchments, which it attributes to forests detaining floodwater through infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1]. Flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies with data on them in a global systematic review of forest restoration and water [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1], and in a US experimental basin the gradual recovery of peak discharges after clear-cutting, as vegetation regrew, is attributed to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. A global study of natural climate solutions also lists flood control among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits, citing an earlier assessment, with no size given [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3].
forest_restoration__cross_family__flood_.conditionality: The flood-cover review pools afforestation, reforestation, woodland and deforestation cases, and its peak-flow points come from other studies' modelled scenarios in mostly temperate catchments, so its rule of thumb is a synthesis of models rather than measured restoration outcomes [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1]. The restoration-and-water review pools explicit and implicit forest restoration with forestry and afforestation, is dominated by temperate and Oceania studies, and reports vote counts rather than effect sizes, so it does not say how large the reduction is or which restoration practice delivers it [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]; the US result is regrowth after a clear-cut, not a restoration project, and does not name a practice [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. No unit comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. Expert positions point the other way: an FAO–CIFOR synthesis concludes that massive forestation programmes proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may bring other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change and settlements, roads and drains remain [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. A review of coastal tree belts adds a coastal null: the science on short-period wave damping should not be taken to show that vegetation can reduce the effects of storm surges [ev_flood_hazard_feagin10_1]; it concerns coastal plantings rather than river floods. The co-benefit listing is second-hand and states no size, place or scale [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3]. None of these is a measurement. Any benefit is off-site for farmers.

forest_restoration__cross_family__heat_s.mechanism: Satellite comparisons of forest gain and loss show that more forest cools the land surface locally in tropical and temperate regions, with the largest cooling where tropical forest cover rose by about 50%, while forest loss warms it [ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_5].
forest_restoration__cross_family__heat_s.conditionality: The cooling is absent in boreal regions [ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_3]. The evidence is a single global remote-sensing study of observed forest-cover change, not of planting or regeneration as such, and land surface temperature is only a proxy for heat stress.

forest_restoration__cross_family__heat_s.mechanism: Gaining forest cover cools the land surface: in a global satellite comparison, forest gain lowered annual land surface temperature by 0.18 degrees C in the tropics and 0.19 degrees C in temperate regions, and forest gain of about 50% in tropical regions led to cooling of 1.11 degrees C [ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_4].
forest_restoration__cross_family__heat_s.conditionality: Boreal regions showed a null effect [ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_3]. All units come from a single satellite study of observed forest-cover change rather than a named restoration practice, and it measures annual land surface temperature rather than heat stress on crops, livestock or people, so the strength is not stated.

forest_restoration__cross_family__produc.mechanism: The evidence points both ways. On the gain side, under the Reflorestar payment programme in Espírito Santo, Brazil, the poorest quarter of municipalities saw agricultural value added rise by 8% and the value of agricultural production by about 14% [ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_3], and a preprint review, not yet peer reviewed, finds that increases in forest cover led to higher landscape-scale agricultural productivity in 95% of reported cases, with gains from 0.4% to 79.5% [ev_crop_yield_yang24_1]. On the loss side, a meta-analysis found that returning cropland or bare land to forest left soil total nitrogen not significantly changed overall (3.04%), but that it decreased by 16.84% in hot regions and by 19.85% in humid regions compared with cropland, which the authors attribute to higher plant uptake of soil nitrogen under high temperature and rainfall [ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_6, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_7].
forest_restoration__cross_family__produc.conditionality: What separates the sides is what is measured and where. The gains are farm production value under a payments programme and landscape-scale yields after forest cover gain; the losses are soil nitrogen on land converted from cropland to forest, confined to hot and humid regions, with no significant change across all sites [ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_6, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_7]. The nitrogen units are part of the production picture rather than a yield measurement. The Brazilian gain holds only for the poorest municipalities, the programme pools forest conservation with regeneration, planting, agroforestry and silvopasture, and municipal production value stands in for the farm production gap in an upper-middle-income setting [ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_2]. The preprint compiles cases where forest cover rose without naming a restoration practice [ev_crop_yield_yang24_1]. No measured unit comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting.

forest_restoration__cross_family__rural_.mechanism: Restored forests can diversify livelihoods and raise income from timber and non-timber forest products [ev_household_income_iufro20_8]; in Wuqi County, China, the sloping land conservation programme increased local incomes by 164 percent and off-farm income by 20 times [ev_household_income_wri17_1], and global estimates put the benefit-cost ratio of restoring degraded forest land at 7.5 to 30.9, including public goods [ev_economic_return_wri17_1, ev_economic_return_wri17_2]. A meta-analysis of payments for environmental services finds a positive effect on overall household income (SMD = 0.25, 95% CI [0.09, 0.41]) [ev_household_income_snilstveit19_1]. A preprint review, not yet peer reviewed, cites economic models suggesting that pollination benefits from forest restoration could fully outweigh its costs, especially in areas already having at least 10% forest cover [ev_economic_return_yang24_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__rural_.conditionality: Restoration can also take agricultural land and reduce on-farm income or employment, the measured harm on this row [ev_household_income_iufro20_7]. Few studies conclusively show that restored-forest benefits alleviate poverty, which occurs over years or decades when it does [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_4], and Brazil's Reflorestar programme showed no significant effect on municipal GDP, value added or employment [ev_economic_return_seixas24_1]. The same payments meta-analysis finds no significant effect on agricultural income (SMD = 0.11), nonagricultural income or household assets [ev_household_income_snilstveit19_2], so the income gain does not show up as farm income or wealth. The Wuqi gain has no counterfactual and is largely off-farm and subsidy-driven, the benefit-cost ratios are global model estimates, the pollination result is a cited model in a preprint, and income and returns stand in for poverty.

forest_restoration__cross_family__soil_e.mechanism: Review statements that name restoration generically, not a single family, sit here. An FAO regional review of forests and landslides in Asia asserts that tree planting on susceptible slopes can reduce risk, and that natural regeneration and tree planting on failed slopes can help control after-effects such as sediment release into rivers [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_1]. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology finds erosion minimal where the soil surface is protected by a well-developed litter and herb layer, only slightly higher without the understorey, and dramatically higher once the litter layer is destroyed or removed, so the protection comes from what lies on the ground [ev_erosion_hazard_bruij90_10]. An FAO forests-and-water synthesis calls forest restoration one of the best ways of restoring productivity and reducing sedimentation in degraded areas of cleared land experiencing accelerated erosion [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1], and lists reducing soil loss and keeping sediment out of streams among the very good reasons for rehabilitating watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. It cites Taiwan, where reservoir sedimentation from 1965 until 1985 was reduced by 55 percent of the base rate, attributed to a rehabilitation programme [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. A meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones finds that both forestland and grassland restoration of cropland or bare land were effective methods for controlling erosion, cutting sediment and runoff, with canopies, root systems and the organic surface layer not differing in their impact [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1, ev_runoff_reduction_yang23_2]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, upstream treatment with deep trenches, percolation pits and afforestation reduced siltation of May Demu dam by up to 60%, a figure the chapter takes from Woldearegay's earlier 2011 report, and in the Abreha Weatsbeha watershed the authors observed significant improvements in reducing soil erosion after afforestation, area closures and water-harvesting works [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. The effect is off-site for farmers: stabilised slopes and less sediment reaching rivers and reservoirs, at slope and catchment scale rather than on the farm plot.
forest_restoration__cross_family__soil_e.conditionality: The class is capped at moderate because few units say how large the effect is: the Taiwan reduction and the Tigray dam figure carry sizes, while the FAO and UNESCO statements are review judgements without a measured value and the erosion-zone meta-analysis reports its forest-only effect sizes only in a figure [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_bruij90_10, ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1]. The UNESCO litter finding pools natural forests, fallows, plantations and tree gardens; it says the soil is protected only while litter and understorey are kept, which is a condition on any restoration, not a guaranteed benefit [ev_erosion_hazard_bruij90_10]. The Tigray results are bundles of afforestation and area closures with trenches, percolation pits and check-dams, from showcase sites, and the dam figure is an upper bound carried from an earlier report, so neither can be credited to tree cover alone [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. The Taiwan reduction is credited to a bundled programme of reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control, check dams and gully control, fruit trees and agroforestry, and conservation farming, so it cannot be attributed to forest restoration alone [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The same synthesis is explicit that achieving substantial flood reduction is not among the reasons to rehabilitate watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. The Tigray units are the only evidence here from a low-income setting. Landslide risk is recorded under erosion here for lack of a landslide category.

forest_restoration__cross_family__water_.mechanism: Both units come from a single FAO forests-and-water synthesis that names restoration generically rather than a single family: forest restoration is described as one of the best ways of restoring productivity and reducing sedimentation in degraded areas of cleared land experiencing accelerated erosion [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1], and in Taiwan reservoir sedimentation from 1965 until 1985 was reduced by 55 percent of the base rate, attributed to a rehabilitation programme [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. Lower sediment load is used here as a component of water quality, and the benefit falls downstream, off-site for farmers.
forest_restoration__cross_family__water_.conditionality: This row is data deficient: it rests on one source, whose general claim is an assertion and whose Taiwan figure is cited second-hand, so it is described here but cannot set a class. The Taiwan programme bundles reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control, check dams and gully control, fruit trees and agroforestry, and conservation farming, so the reduction cannot be credited to restoration alone, and it is a high-income case [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. What is missing is a second independent source or a measured water-quality finding, ideally from a low- or lower-middle-income catchment.

forest_restoration__cross_family__water_.mechanism: Expanding forest cover moves water in two opposite directions within the same review. More water gets into the soil: in 83% of the studies reporting on infiltration capacity or soil infiltration, infiltration increased [ev_soil_permeability_filoso17_1]. Less reaches groundwater: in 67% of the studies with data on groundwater levels or recharge, groundwater decreased with forest cover expansion [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__water_.conditionality: The two sides are measuring different things, soil infiltration and groundwater, and the evidence does not say which drives water stress for a given user. A farmer depending on soil moisture and a household depending on wells or springs fed by recharge would read them differently; the groundwater decrease is a measured harm for the latter. Timing also separates them: aboveground benefits recover within a few years, but infiltration and recharge are counted in decades rather than years [ev_soil_permeability_iufro18_1], an expert panel conclusion rather than a measurement. The review pools forestry and afforestation with restoration, is dominated by temperate and Oceania studies, and reports vote counts rather than sizes. Water leaving the catchment for downstream users is covered by the catchment water yield rows.

forest_restoration__drought__all.mechanism: Every sub-practice row that votes here finds forest restoration eases drought only a little, apart from the protection and community forest management row, and the vote, not the pooled count of beneficial units, sets the low class. In the protection and community forest management row, the India compiler credits the watershed programme with improved surface and subsurface hydrological functioning in the upper watershed, which raised springshed groundwater stores and dry-season stream and spring flows [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_drought_impacts]. In Malawi, households taking part in forest co-management through village natural resource management committees had 57% higher annual forestry income after a rainfall shock than non-participants [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_4], and under shocks the per capita income gain from participation showed up among moderately poor households, at 31.4% [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_7]. In the passive regeneration row, households in Tigray, Ethiopia, downstream of exclosures harvested 188 to 222 kg/ha more than households beside open grazing areas in the drought-affected 2023 season [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_1]. The cross-family row rests on a meta-analysis of Ethiopian catchment restoration reporting that exclosures, tree planting, bunds and terraces reduce water losses and improve water in soils, rivers and aquifers [ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1]. The pool also holds a Niger rating that assisted natural regeneration, by improving vegetation cover and woody production, helps reduce the impacts of long droughts in the rainy season, and a regional model of large-scale reforestation that found fewer extremely dry months in 9 of 15 regions [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1].
forest_restoration__drought__all.conditionality: The effect is off-site for farmers: the Tigray yield advantage compares exclosures with open grazing, so it measures a downstream benefit to cropland rather than production on the restored land, and it was larger in the drier first year than in the following year [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_3]. The co-management benefit is confined to forest income: participation did not mitigate the effect of rainfall shocks on non-forestry income, which shocks are likely to erode by 36% among participating households too, and this no-benefit result is what discounts the class [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_5]. The per capita gain under shocks reached moderately poor households rather than the poorest, and the authors report it as shifting away from the poorest decile [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_7]. The India reading rests on a compiler rating rather than a measurement, and the cross-family evidence bundles exclosure and planting with bunds and terraces [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_drought_impacts, ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1]. forest_restoration__food_insecurity.mechanism: Restoration and co-managed forest improve food security mainly through more fodder, water and forest foods around regenerating sites, though the measured gain is small. forest_restoration__passive_regeneration.mechanism: Natural regeneration rebuilds biodiversity strongly as secondary forest develops. Across tropical chronosequences species richness recovers fastest and composition slowest, with richness after 20 years at 78% of old-growth values [ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_2]; tree species richness in Brazil's Atlantic Forest rises with time since disturbance [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1]; and in the western Andes of Colombia restored bird and dung beetle communities closely resembled those of old growth forests after 15–30 yr [ev_biodiversity_outcome_chazdon16_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis finds natural regeneration outperforms active planting for plants, birds and invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1], and in Senegal's southern Groundnut Basin woody species richness in exclosures rose from 27 species after 1 year to 51 species after 5 and 12 years, an increase of more than 52% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1].
forest_restoration__passive_regeneration.conditionality: Recovery of composition and endemism is slow: composition after 20 years was only 33% of old-growth values [ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_1], and in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest regaining mature-forest endemism was estimated to take 1987 years [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_3]. A global meta-analysis found biodiversity in naturally regenerated forests lower than in reference forests for every class of socioeconomic, biogeographic and ecological factor it examined [ev_biodiversity_outcome_latawiec16_1]; that comparison is with old-growth or less-disturbed forest, not with the degraded land regeneration starts from, so it is held out of the class as a recovery shortfall, not a loss caused by regeneration. The pantropical meta-analysis compares regeneration with planting rather than with degraded land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1], and the Senegal result compares exclosures of different ages at one site rather than exclosures with open grazed land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. The gain accrues to the regenerating forest and the landscape, not to the adopting farmer's fields.

forest_restoration__passive_regeneration.mechanism: Secondary forest regrowing on cleared or abandoned land adds carbon in biomass and soil. A global meta-analysis gives natural regeneration removal rates of 9.1–18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. A pantropical synthesis of field plots gives above-ground biomass growth of up to 7.6 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year in younger African rainforest stands, falling to 0.5 in older subtropical Asian mountain stands [ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_22]. Global models estimate an average regrowth rate of 3.16 Mg C per hectare per year, with mapped rates from 0.058 to 6 [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_1], a median 30-year accumulation of 60.2 tC per hectare in biomass and soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_1], 51 t of above-ground carbon per hectare in a 20-year-old moist tropical forest [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch19_1], and 23.4 Gt of C over 215 Mha in 30 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1]. Field chronosequences agree: Amazon secondary forests held 50% (229 t/ha) of mature forest biomass after 25 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_gehring05_1], Colombian Andean regrowth reached about half of old-growth carbon within 15–30 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_chazdon16_1], and an Atlantic Forest fragment regrown for 60 years reached 297 Mg/ha against 313 Mg/ha in preserved forest nearby [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_5]. Soil carbon recovers fastest, reaching 90% of old-growth values in about 5 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_poorter21_1], with average gains of 0.447% of pre-transition soil carbon per year [ev_soil_organic_carbon_busch19_1].
forest_restoration__passive_regeneration.conditionality: Above-ground biomass recovers slowly, taking 12 decades by one pantropical estimate [ev_carbon_sequestration_poorter21_1], so a project cycle captures only the early part of the gain. Much of the size evidence is modelled: the global regrowth rates are model outputs for above-ground carbon, assume steady growth over 30 years, and the soil rate of 0.42 Mg C per hectare per year is a default its authors say needs further research [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cookpatton20_3]; the global potential holds only if regrowing forests can establish and persist [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1]. evidence_summary: Chazdon 2016 (cited review, tropics): naturally regenerating forests are an important source of timber and non-timber products supporting local livelihoods.
A study of coastal Atlantic forest in south-east Brazil: secondary forest regeneration combined with harvesting a local palm fruit improved farmer income, soil quality and forest structure.
A WOCAT expert case (low-income context): farm income rose through selling grass and wood from the regenerating area.

A meta-analysis from Ethiopia finds areas closed for grazing and agriculture had runoff coefficients of 4% against 19% on control sites [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1], and in Leyte, Philippines, recovering forest on former slash-and-burn land generated the smallest share of overland flow among the land uses compared [ev_runoff_reduction_sidle06_1]. On harvested slopes, the higher probability of landslides following timber removal diminishes substantially 15–25 yr after harvesting as replacement trees mature [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2], and a global forest-water assessment adds that land abandonment with expanding forest and grassland has in some cases decreased soil erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_5].

Regrowth is slow to restore slope protection: young second-growth timber falls far short of providing the root support that its much larger and older predecessors did [ev_erosion_hazard_bishop64_5], and the landslide recovery result tracks regrowth after timber harvest, not a restoration project, without separating replanting from natural regeneration [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2]. Apart from these reviews and the Ethiopian meta-analysis, which measures runoff as a component of erosion, the remaining units are Tanzanian compiler ratings rather than measurements, and the Ethiopian closures are compared with open control sites rather than isolating regrowth from other changes in use [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1].
